# Local resolution weighted composite of Martigny

This tutorial runs the whole pipeline, from search to composites, for an area
around Martigny in the Swiss canton of Valais. The town is surrounded by
mountains, whose steep slopes are challenging terrain for SAR. The tutorial
compares a composite of the ascending orbits, one of the descending orbits,
and one that combines both with local resolution weighting (LRW).

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

from dotenv import load_dotenv

root = next(p for p in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents) if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists())
load_dotenv(root / ".env")
(root / "cache/docs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
os.chdir(root / "cache/docs")
```

## Find the grid squares and their bursts

The area touches four 10 km squares of the MGRS grid, all in UTM zone 32
North. The search covers the squares whole, as in
[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#find-the-bursts-of-every-square),
and returns every VV burst of August 2025 that reaches them:

```{python}
import shapely
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import (
    BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter,
    RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange,
)

fm = FileManager("data/martigny")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
aoi = box(7.03, 46.06, 7.12, 46.14)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
squares = list(MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20))
print(", ".join(square.mgrs_code for square in squares), {str(square.crs) for square in squares})

search_area = shapely.union_all([box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox) for square in squares])
bursts = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV"))

bursts.df.groupby(["pass_direction", "rel_orbit_number"]).agg(
    acquisitions=("date", lambda dates: dates.dt.date.nunique()),
    bursts=("burst_id", "size"),
    sub_swaths=("sub_swath", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.unique()))),
    satellites=("parent_product_name", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.str[:3].unique()))),
)
```

One ascending and two descending orbits cover the squares, each imaged five
times in August, with 50 bursts in total.

## Process the bursts

The squares share one zone, so all bursts are processed in one batch in that
zone, at the 20 m pixel size of the composites:

```{python}
#| output: false
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=squares[0].crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20),
).raise_on_failure().products
```

## Compose every square

Each square is composed twice: once per pass direction with
`compose_rtc_by_pass()`, and once across both directions with
`compose_rtc_lrw()`, which also writes the quality layers.

```{python}
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
lrw, by_pass = [], []
for square in squares:
    footprints = {(b.burst_id, b.sub_swath) for b in bursts.intersecting(square)}
    square_rtc = [p for p in rtc if (p.burst_id, p.sub_swath) in footprints]
    lrw.append(weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(square_rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window))
    by_pass.append(weighter.compose_rtc_by_pass(square_rtc, square, time_range=window))
    print(f"{square.mgrs_code}: {len(square_rtc)} bursts")
```

## Compare the viewing directions

Sentinel-1 looks to the right of its track: east on ascending passes, west on
descending ones. A slope facing the radar is squeezed into few pixels and seen
coarsely. A slope facing away is stretched and seen finely, unless it is so
steep that it lies in radar shadow, where that direction has no value.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Backscatter composites of August 2025 in a 4 by 4 km window west of Martigny: the five ascending acquisitions (left), the ten descending acquisitions (middle), and all fifteen combined with LRW (right). White marks radar shadow, where a composite has no value."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from rasterio.merge import merge
from s1bursts.product import Layer


def mosaic(composites, layer=Layer.MEASUREMENT):
    """Join the squares of one layer; return the data and its transform."""
    data, transform = merge([fm.get_product_path(c, layer) for c in composites])
    return data[0].astype("float32"), transform


def km_extent(data, transform):
    """Return the extent of a mosaic in kilometers, for imshow."""
    rows, cols = data.shape
    left, top = transform.c, transform.f
    return [v / 1000 for v in (left, left + transform.a * cols, top + transform.e * rows, top)]


view = (346.5, 350.5, 5106, 5110)  # easting and northing in km, UTM zone 32N
composites = {
    "Ascending": mosaic([c["Ascending"] for c in by_pass]),
    "Descending": mosaic([c["Descending"] for c in by_pass]),
    "LRW": mosaic(lrw),
}
viridis = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
viridis.set_bad("white")  # pixels without a value: radar shadow

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.2), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (name, (data, transform)) in zip(axes, composites.items()):
    image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(data), extent=km_extent(data, transform),
                      cmap=viridis, vmin=-15, vmax=0)
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Gamma-0 (dB)")
plt.show()
```

Each pass composite has gaps on the steep slopes facing away from its
direction, and smears the slopes facing it into coarse streaks. The LRW
composite has a value everywhere, and on each slope it leans toward the
direction that sees the slope finely.

## Read the quality layers

The LRW composite comes with two quality layers, shown here for the same
window:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The LRW composite (left), the number of acquisitions that contributed to each pixel, QA-NUM (middle), and the composite quality, QA-CQM, in decibels (right)."
layers = {
    "LRW composite (dB)": (Layer.MEASUREMENT, dict(cmap="viridis", vmin=-15, vmax=0)),
    "QA-NUM": (Layer.QA_NUM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=15)),
    "QA-CQM (dB)": (Layer.QA_CQM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=-8, vmax=8)),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.8), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (title, (layer, style)) in zip(axes, layers.items()):
    data, transform = mosaic(lrw, layer)
    if layer != Layer.QA_NUM:
        data = 10 * np.log10(data)
    fig.colorbar(ax.imshow(data, extent=km_extent(data, transform), **style), ax=ax,
                 orientation="horizontal")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
plt.show()
```

`QA-NUM` counts the acquisitions that contribute to each pixel: all fifteen
almost everywhere, fewer where one direction sees only radar shadow. `QA-CQM`
rates the combined resolution of each pixel. It is highest on slopes that some
orbits see from behind and lowest on the steepest slopes, which every orbit
sees squeezed or not at all. A pixel with a low `QA-CQM` describes the ground
more coarsely than its 20 m pixel size suggests.
[Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains both layers.
